summaries.example: Imagine two clues: “the star seen in the morning” and “the star seen in the evening.” They can point to the same planet, Venus, but they give us different information. Learning that the two clues point to one planet can teach us something new.
summaries.summary: Intensional logic studies an important difference between what words mean and what they point to. For example, “morning star” and “evening star” point to Venus, but they do not present Venus in the same way. In a simple sentence, replacing one phrase with another phrase for the same object may leave the truth unchanged. But in a sentence about what someone knows, believes, or finds surprising, the replacement may change the sentence. This shows that meaning matters in some settings. Logicians call meaning an intension and what an expression points to its extension. They build formal systems using states or possible worlds to represent different situations. Some systems treat an intension as something that can point to different objects in different states. Other approaches describe meaning as a procedure or algorithm for working out a result. The history of these ideas includes major work by Frege, Church, Carnap, Marcus, Montague, Tichý, Bressan, Gallin, and others.
key_ideas: A phrase can point to the same thing as another phrase while having a different meaning.
Intensional logic studies both meaning and what expressions point to.
In statements about knowing or believing, replacing one phrase with another can sometimes change what is true.
Possible worlds or states help logicians describe how meanings may point to different things in different situations.
summaries.why_it_matters: We often understand language by more than matching words with objects. We also care about clues, ways of presenting things, knowledge, belief, possibility, and information. Intensional logic gives philosophers and logicians tools for thinking carefully about these differences. It also helps explain why ordinary language can be harder to formalize than straightforward mathematical statements.

important_terms.definition: What an expression means or the way it presents something to us.
The thing, object, or truth value that an expression points to.
A setting where meaning matters, not only what an expression points to. Knowledge and belief are examples.
A setting where replacing one expression with another expression for the same thing does not change the result.

questions_to_think_about: Can two clues point to the same object but teach you different facts?
Why might replacing a name in a sentence about someone’s knowledge cause trouble?
Would a computer need to track both meanings and objects to understand language?

summaries.example: Suppose a student knows that “the tallest person in the room” is Alex, but does not know that Alex is the oldest person there. If, by coincidence, Alex is both tallest and oldest, the two descriptions have the same extension in that situation. Still, the student may not know that the descriptions pick out the same person. A logic that tracks only extensions would miss this difference.
summaries.summary: Intensional logic investigates the relation between an expression’s intension—its meaning or mode of presentation—and its extension, what it designates. The distinction becomes visible when co-referring expressions behave differently inside larger sentences. “Morning star” and “evening star” designate Venus, yet someone can learn that they co-designate. Likewise, a person may know one description of an object without knowing an equivalent description. In extensional contexts, substitution of co-designating expressions generally preserves truth; in intensional contexts involving knowledge, belief, information, surprise, or modality, it may not. Frege supplied a foundational distinction between sense and reference. Church developed a formal logic with separate treatment of senses and denotations. Carnap gave intensions a semantic representation as assignments of extensions across possible states. Marcus developed quantified modal systems and defended a tag-like treatment of names. Montague, Tichý, Bressan, and Gallin extended possible-world and type-theoretic approaches, often treating intensions functionally. The entry also discusses first-order intensional logic, varying and constant domains, partial designations, definite descriptions, and the de re/de dicto distinction. Rigidity makes some cases difficult, especially mathematical identities and proper names. A different line of work, associated with Moschovakis, models sense as an algorithm whose execution yields a denotation. These approaches illuminate different parts of the problem rather than producing one final solution.
key_ideas: Frege’s sense/reference distinction motivates the central problem: co-referring expressions can differ in cognitive significance.
Classical first-order logic is mainly extensional, so formalizing knowledge, belief, necessity, and informative identity requires richer systems.
Carnap models intensions as functions assigning extensions across states, while other approaches treat senses as more independent or as algorithms.
Modal semantics distinguishes possible or accessible states and can represent necessity, possibility, and epistemic alternatives.
Rigid names create a special problem: if two names necessarily designate the same object, their identity can still be discovered empirically rather than known automatically.
There is no single completely successful intensional logic; different systems handle different phenomena and introduce different technical complications.
summaries.why_it_matters: The difference between meaning and designation appears in philosophy of language, modal logic, epistemic logic, mathematics, and formal theories of computation. It explains why two true identities can differ in informativeness, why knowledge cannot always be modeled by truth alone, and why ordinary descriptions do not behave like proper names. Studying intensional logic also shows how formal models must choose what counts as a state, which objects exist in each state, which expressions designate, and how meanings are represented.

important_terms.definition: The meaning, sense, or mode of presentation associated with an expression. In some approaches, it is modeled as a function from states to extensions.
What an expression designates in a particular state; for a sentence, this may be its truth value.
A context in which substitution of expressions with the same extension can fail to preserve truth, especially contexts involving knowledge, belief, or necessity.
A context in which expressions with the same extension can normally be substituted without affecting truth.
A mathematically represented state or possible world relative to which a formula, object, or expression is evaluated.
A distinction between applying possibility or necessity to an object across states and applying it to a whole statement within alternative states.
An expression whose designation stays the same across the relevant states.
A procedure or structured method of evaluation proposed as a way to model the sense of an expression.

questions_to_think_about: Why does “Venus is Venus” usually provide less information than “the morning star is the evening star,” even when both involve the same planet?
Should a model of knowledge represent only what is true, or also how a person has access to that truth?
How might epistemic possible worlds differ from worlds representing metaphysical necessity?
Can an algorithm capture every kind of meaning, especially when its evaluation may not finish?
What should a logic say about a description that fails to designate anything?

summaries.example: Maya knows that “the first person to finish the race” finished before noon. She does not know that Jordan finished before noon. Later she learns that Jordan was the first person to finish. The two expressions referred to the same person, but substituting one for the other inside a sentence about Maya’s knowledge changed what Maya knows.
summaries.summary: Intensional logic studies cases in which what an expression means matters in addition to what it refers to. “Morning star” and “evening star,” for instance, can refer to the same planet while presenting it differently. In an ordinary factual sentence, replacing one with the other may preserve truth. In a sentence about someone’s knowledge or belief, however, the substitution may fail: a person can know one description without knowing the other describes the same object. This is why such settings are called intensional contexts. The subject grew from Frege’s distinction between sense and reference. Church tried to formalize separate senses and denotations. Carnap represented an intension by assigning an extension to an expression at each possible state. Later logicians developed modal, quantified, and higher-type systems, with different choices about domains and about how expressions designate across states. The entry also considers descriptions that designate only in some states, the difference between de re and de dicto readings, and the special behavior of rigid names. Mathematical expressions create another challenge: “1 + 4” and “2 + 3” have the same answer but may involve different procedures or information. Algorithmic approaches try to represent such procedures as senses. The larger lesson is that no simple rule captures every relation among meaning, reference, truth, knowledge, and possibility.
key_ideas: The same object can be presented through different meanings, and this difference can affect what someone knows.
Intensional logic was developed because ordinary language includes contexts that classical extensional logic does not represent well.
Frege’s sense and reference, Carnap’s state-based intensions, and Church’s formal sense-denotation system are important stages in the subject’s history.
Modal logic uses accessible states to analyze necessity and possibility, but the meaning of those states depends on whether they represent alternative realities, times, or knowledge situations.
Proper names and mathematical expressions are difficult because they can be rigid or have the same output in every state while still differing in how people learn them.
Some theories treat meaning as a structured procedure or algorithm rather than only as a state-by-state mapping.
summaries.why_it_matters: People communicate with descriptions, names, proofs, clues, and assumptions—not just with bare objects. Intensional logic helps explain why learning that two descriptions co-refer can be informative, why statements about belief resist simple substitution, and why possibility and necessity need careful interpretation. It also connects philosophical questions about language with formal tools used in logic and the study of computation.

important_terms.definition: The meaning or way an expression presents something, rather than merely the thing it points to.
The object, property, or truth value an expression points to in a particular situation.
A sentence setting involving knowledge, belief, possibility, or similar ideas, where meaning can affect truth.
A sentence setting where expressions pointing to the same thing can usually replace one another without changing truth.
A possible situation used by logicians to evaluate what is true, possible, or necessary.
An expression that keeps the same designation across the relevant possible worlds.
A way to separate “the object has a possible property” from “it is possible that the description has that property.”

questions_to_think_about: Can two expressions refer to the same person while differing in what a character knows?
When does replacing an expression with an equal one seem safe, and when does it seem suspicious?
Should “possible worlds” represent different realities, different times, or different information states?
Why might a name and a description need different rules in a logical system?
Would two different methods that always produce the same answer have the same meaning?
